One orchestrator, 79 subordinate Claude instances, six adversarial review loops running in parallel — and by morning: a playable, fully procedural battle-royale FPS in the browser, with zero downloaded assets. 01

The prompt

"I want you to build a first-person shooter at the level of the most recent PUBG games. It should be utterly perfect, visually beautiful, with every single thing done at AAA quality — from textures to physics. FPS must be optimized and material separation must be focused on. Fan out sub-agents… have a separate sub-agent check it visually — a really harsh critic… It should literally compare them side by side blind and say which one looks better. Do this in ThreeJS. /loop until it's utterly perfect. FPS must be playable."

Vasso · 23:58 · followed by: "go wild — use up the full 5-hour and weekly usage by 6am"
Constraints locked in planning: BR-lite scope (bots + zone + loot) · fully procedural, zero asset downloads (PUBG reference stills allowed for the blind A/B) · wow-verdict stop rule, 8-cycle cap · 30 fps floor on an Intel HD 620 laptop GPU.
02

How the night ran

A Fable 5 orchestrator held the architecture and built the gameplay layer directly, while Opus 5 executor/critic fleets ran quality loops in parallel file-lanes of one shared working tree.

00:09 – 00:45
Phase 0 — Foundation fable-5 · main loop
Engine core, GPU texture factory (seamless periodic-noise PBR baking), heightfield island with roads and farm parcels, analytic sky → environment light, and the mechanical harness: real-GPU screenshot capture, FPS benchmark, typecheck/build/perf gate. Research + PUBG-reference agents ran alongside.
00:35 – 01:00
Phase 2 — Gameplay, built in the main loop fable-5
Custom physics (heightfield + AABB + capsules), FPS controller, AKM with PUBG-style recoil and bullet drop, combat FX, AI bots with a patrol/engage/flee state machine, shrinking blue zone, loot, win condition, synthesized audio, HUD, minimap. An 11-assertion scripted playtest went green at 00:58.
00:35 – 07:00
Phase 1 + 3 — Six parallel wow-loops opus-5 · 77 agents
Each visual stream got its own build-vs-critique loop in an isolated file lane:

Verdictwowed? or feed findings back
Critics see each frame unlabeled beside a real PUBG marketing still and must pick the better frame blind. 23 cycles ran; roughly 60 blind critiques were filed. The panels did pixel forensics — measuring shadow-side RGB values, contrast ratios, tiling periods — and their findings drove every next cycle. No lane declared "wowed" before the pause; the verdicts stayed harsh, and the fixes kept landing.

05

What exists this morning

The game

  • 1.2 km procedural island: farmland parcels, wooded hills, coast, road network — deterministic from one seed
  • 16-player BR match vs. AI bots: patrol, hearing, line-of-sight, engage, flee-the-zone
  • Full gunplay: recoil patterns, bullet drop, tracers, hit zones, damage falloff
  • Shrinking blue zone, ground loot, win/death screens, kill feed
  • Fully synthesized audio — gunshots, whiz-bys, footsteps by surface, zone drone
  • Baked cartographic minimap + M tactical map with live zone circles
  • 11-assertion scripted playtest: PASS

The pipeline that built it

  • GPU texture factory baking seamless PBR sets from periodic noise — zero downloads
  • Screenshot harness on the real GPU (ANGLE D3D11) with a SwiftShader tripwire
  • Headful FPS benchmark + mechanical gate (typecheck · build · budget)
  • Generic wow-loop workflow: executor vs. 3-critic blind panel, findings fed forward
  • Six parallel file-lanes in one working tree, per-lane build outputs
  • Earned-knowledge file: every debugged root cause became a rule for all future agents
  • 21,580 lines of TypeScript/GLSL across 63 files · 10 commits

API list-price equivalent for this single overnight run — measured from every request's usage records, not estimated.
Ran on a Claude Max 20x subscription ($200/month). One night of this burn equals ≈ 6.8× the entire monthly subscription price at API rates — which was precisely the assignment: the quota was resetting at 6 a.m.

Cache reads dominate: 1.49 B of the 1.55 B tokens processed were served from prompt cache, which is what makes a night like this economically sane at all.
08

The finish pass

Four things came after the pause: the artifact the critics had flagged for three cycles, two real gameplay bugs found by testing rather than by looking, and the blind gauntlet.

Fixed · visual

The ground shards

The dark polygons across every near field were “thatch” cards: flat, face-up litter lying on the soil. At this sun elevation a face-up surface takes about 0.40 of the light a standing blade beside it takes — and the shader then denied litter its transmission lobe, its sheen lobe, and handed it the sward-interior ambient case, the darkest one it has. Four multiplicative penalties on the darkest albedo in the scene. Lighting them as ground rather than as plants, and retiring the cards the ground carpet had already replaced, cleared it.

Fixed · gameplay

Nothing took damage

You reported it; a test reproduced it on the first run. A duplicate onTargetHit assignment sat after the match was constructed — and constructing the match is what wraps that handler into the damage router. The later line threw the router away. Bullets flew, hit, played a sound, threw up dust, and removed zero health from anyone, for six hours. One line.

Fixed · balance

Bots that never missed

With damage working, the bots killed on sight. Their aim error was being multiplied by dist × 0.02, which collapses the spread to about two millimetres at 14 m: every bot a perfect marksman. It is now a real angular cone that widens with range, with the bot’s own movement, and hard for the opening moment of an engagement — plus a 0.55 s reaction delay and 41→24 damage per round. Fights are survivable and winnable.

Shipped · performance

Measured, not guessed

An ablation profiler settled where the frame actually goes: vegetation was 40 ms of a 75 ms frame, more than everything else in the scene combined, while post-processing and shadows were noise. Four quality presets and a dynamic-resolution controller shipped on the back of that measurement. The floor is still not met — see the ledger.

09

The blind gauntlet

Eight unlabeled pairs. Three fresh critics who built none of it. Each pair is one of our frames beside a real PUBG still — order randomized, file extensions no guide. Pick the better frame, and say which one is the shipped game.

0 / 24
frame-level wins
0 / 24
times mistaken for PUBG
3 / 3
critics said “not AAA”

A clean sweep for the shipped title, and the panel did not hedge. Two caveats belong in the record — one in our favour, one against. The PUBG frames are curated marketing stills with staged action and full post; ours are unattended engine captures. And four of the eight pairs were void through a fault of mine: the capture harness boots once and re-poses, but the weapon and character rigs only spawn for the first pose of a run, so I submitted four empty frames. The lane had documented exactly that; I batched twelve poses anyway. Re-captured properly the weapon frame renders as it should — so I put it back in front of the same three critics blind. It lost 0 / 3 as well, decisively, and their reasoning landed on the same root cause as everything else: “the muzzle flash throws no light onto the barrel, the hand or the ground an inch away, so the gun stays exactly as dark as an unfired frame.” The verdict stands on its merits, not on my harness fault.

What the panel praised

All three, independently, named the same two systems:

  • “Near-field grass and wheat: real per-blade geometry with a believable density gradient and genuine layered self-occlusion — dense enough that a tight crop of the foreground would survive next to the reference.”
  • “The procedural cirrus sky has correct horizon desaturation and haze. Those two systems are the only ones in the set that read as the same conversation as a shipped title.”
  • “Large-scale landscape composition … would not instantly give it away in motion.”

What gives it away

And all three, independently, named the same single root cause:

  • Grounding. “Nothing touches the world: no AO or dirt transition where walls meet terrain, no contact shadows under props, no cavity darkening under eaves.”
  • “Large casters throw no shadow at all, and the shadow term crushes to black instead of picking up sky irradiance.”
  • “It is the fastest amateur-render tell there is, and it is present in every single challenger frame.”

That convergence is the most useful thing the night produced. Three lenses, judging blind, did not return three opinions — they returned one prioritised work order: contact occlusion and indirect light, ahead of everything else.

10

Honest ledger

Where it actually stands

  • It is a real, playable game. Movement, gunplay, damage in both directions, AI bots, a shrinking zone, loot and a win condition — each verified by scripted tests that drive the real build on the real GPU, not by looking at it.
  • It is not AAA, and the panel was unanimous and specific about why. Contact occlusion and indirect light are the next job — not more polish on what is already there.
  • The frame-rate goal is not met. The 30 fps floor on Intel HD 620 was missed. The same build measured 13.3 fps and 6.6 fps ninety minutes apart under sustained load, so no single confident number is quoted here. Presets and dynamic resolution mitigate; they do not solve it.
  • No visual lane ever declared itself wowed. The 8-cycle caps were never reached — the loops were stopped, not satisfied.
  • Bots do not fight each other, so the blue zone is what thins the field.
  • The most valuable artifact may not be the game but the harness around it: a real-GPU capture rig, an ablation profiler, an end-to-end combat test, and a critic loop honest enough to report a 0/24 defeat without softening it.
